questions.q: What happens to a Pod's local container filesystem when the Pod is deleted and rescheduled?
options: It is automatically copied to the new Pod by the kubelet
It moves with the Pod to whichever node it is rescheduled on
Kubernetes pauses the writable layer until the new Pod starts, then resumes it
It is gone; the new Pod starts from the image with a brand-new, empty writable layer
questions.explain: A Pod's own filesystem is disposable by design — rescheduling starts a fresh container from the image with a new, empty writable layer, which is why anything needing durable data needs a PersistentVolume instead.

options: A cluster-scoped object representing a real piece of provisioned storage, created independently of any one workload
A field inside a Pod spec that marks a container as stateful
A namespaced request for a given amount of storage
A Helm chart value that sets the disk size for a Deployment
questions.explain: A PV represents an actual piece of storage such as an Azure Disk or AWS EBS volume. It exists independently of any namespace or Pod, unlike a PVC.

questions.q: In a Pod's `volumes` block, what does a Pod actually reference to use persistent storage?
options: The diskURI of the underlying cloud disk directly
The PersistentVolumeClaim's name, not the PersistentVolume directly
The StorageClass name only, with no claim involved
The node name where the disk is physically attached
questions.explain: A Pod mounts a volume by referencing a persistentVolumeClaim's claimName. The indirection through a PVC is what lets the same Pod manifest run against different backing storage in different clusters.

questions.q: A PVC requesting 10Gi stays stuck in `Pending` and never binds. Based on this lesson, what is the most likely cause?
options: PVCs can never bind to PVs created manually, only to dynamically provisioned ones
The Pod using the PVC has not been created yet
No existing PV satisfies the request — wrong size, incompatible accessModes, or no StorageClass available to provision one automatically
The cluster administrator must manually type "bind" for every claim
questions.explain: A claim stuck Pending almost always means the control plane found no matching PV to bind to, whether because of a size/accessMode mismatch or because no default StorageClass exists to dynamically provision one.

questions.q: Why would a PVC requesting `ReadWriteMany` fail to bind against a PV backed by an Azure Disk?
options: Azure Disk is block storage attached to a single VM and only supports ReadWriteOnce, not concurrent multi-node read-write access
ReadWriteMany is not a valid accessMode value in Kubernetes
Azure Disk volumes can only be used by Pods running as root
ReadWriteMany requires the PVC and PV to be in the same namespace, which Azure Disk does not support
questions.explain: accessModes describe mount concurrency, not permissions. Block storage like Azure Disk or AWS EBS only supports ReadWriteOnce; ReadWriteMany needs storage built for concurrent multi-node writers, such as Azure Files or NFS.
